options: A child has SEN only if they have a diagnosed medical condition
A child has a learning difficulty if they have a significantly greater difficulty in learning than the majority of others of the same age
A disability is defined as a physical or mental impairment that has a substantial and long-term adverse effect on ability to carry out normal day-to-day activities
Schools must make 'reasonable adjustments' for pupils with disabilities under the Equality Act 2010

bank.question: What does 'interleaving' mean in the context of lesson planning and revision?
bank.explanation: Interleaving involves mixing different topics or problem types within a single practice session, which improves long-term retention and problem-solving
options: Mixing different topics or skills within a single practice session
Focusing on one specific skill until it is perfectly mastered
Providing students with a 'break' between every ten minutes of work
Teaching two different subjects at the exact same time

bank.question: Pupil Premium funding is specifically allocated to schools to help improve the educational outcomes of disadvantaged pupils
bank.explanation: Looked-after children (LAC) and those who have been LAC are eligible for Pupil Premium Plus, which is higher than the standard Pupil Premium rate

bank.question: Which section of the UK Teachers' Standards outlines the requirement for teachers to 'uphold public trust in the profession'?
bank.explanation: Part 2 of the Teachers' Standards sets out the 'Personal and Professional Conduct' expected of teachers, including maintaining public trust
options: Standard 3 (Demonstrate good subject and curriculum knowledge)
Standard 5 (Adapt teaching to respond to strengths and needs)
Part 2 (Personal and Professional Conduct)
The School Teachers' Pay and Conditions Document (STPCD)

bank.question: Which of the following is an example of the 'Concrete' stage in the CPA approach to mathematics?
bank.explanation: Concrete, Pictorial, Abstract (CPA) uses physical objects to build mental models before moving to symbols
options: Providing children with advanced calculators to solve complex problems
Moving from physical objects to drawings before using abstract symbols
Prioritising rote memorisation of times tables over conceptual understanding
Teaching all mathematical concepts through text-heavy word problems

bank.question: In education, what is meant by the 'halo effect' in teacher assessment?
bank.explanation: The 'halo effect' occurs when a teacher's overall positive impression of a student influences their evaluation of that student's specific work or traits
options: The impact of high expectations on student performance
The tendency for students to copy the behaviour of popular peers
A cognitive bias where one positive trait influences the perception of other traits
A method of seating students in a circle to encourage discussion

bank.question: Which two statements correctly distinguish between 'Summative' and 'Formative' assessment?. (Select 2)
bank.explanation: Summative assessment evaluates learning at the end of a unit, whereas formative assessment is an ongoing process to adapt teaching. The correct answers are Summative assessment evaluates pupil learning at the end of an instructional unit against a standard and Formative assessment is an ongoing process used to adapt teaching and learning in real-time.
options: Summative assessment evaluates pupil learning at the end of an instructional unit against a standard
Formative assessment is an ongoing process used to adapt teaching and learning in real-time
Summative assessment is primarily used to provide instant verbal feedback during a lesson
Formative assessment must always be recorded as a formal grade in the school's tracking system

bank.question: What is the 'expert blind spot' in the context of pedagogical content knowledge?
bank.explanation: The 'expert blind spot' is a cognitive bias where experts find it difficult to predict how hard a task will be for a novice to learn
options: The difficulty experts have in understanding how a novice perceives a task
A teacher's inability to see students in the back corner of a classroom
The failure to notice small errors in a highly familiar curriculum plan
The tendency to ignore student feedback that contradicts a teacher's beliefs

bank.question: Interleaving involves mixing different topics or types of practice within a single lesson or over a series of lessons to improve long-term retention
bank.explanation: This strategy, known as interleaved practice, helps pupils better distinguish between different types of problems or concepts compared to blocked practice

bank.question: According to 'Keeping Children Safe in Education' (KCSIE), how should staff treat 'child-on-child abuse'?
bank.explanation: The KCSIE 2023 guidance states that child-on-child abuse should never be dismissed as just 'banter' or 'part of growing up'
options: It should be treated as a normal part of adolescent development
It should never be dismissed as 'banter' or 'part of growing up'
It is primarily a matter for parents rather than the school's DSL
It only requires official reporting if it occurs off school premises

bank.question: What is the primary benefit of 'interleaving' during student practice?
bank.explanation: Interleaving involves mixing different topics or skills within one study session to improve long-term retention
options: Teaching one single topic until it is completely mastered
Grouping similar types of problems together in one lesson
Providing students with the answers before they attempt the task
Mixing different topics or problem types within a single practice session

bank.question: Which of the following describes a key characteristic of 'working memory'?
bank.explanation: The working memory has a very limited capacity, generally thought to hold around 4 to 7 items of information at a time
options: It can store an infinite amount of information for short periods
It is the area where permanent memories are stored for later use
It is unaffected by the complexity of the information being processed
It has a very limited capacity for holding and manipulating information

bank.question: According to Part 2 of the Teachers' Standards (Personal and Professional Conduct), which three behaviours are expected of teachers?. (Select 3)
bank.explanation: Teachers' Standards demand high professional conduct, including tolerance of others' beliefs and neutrality on personal views. The correct answers are Showing tolerance of and respect for the rights of others, Ensuring that personal beliefs are not expressed in ways which exploit pupils' vulnerability and Maintaining high standards in their own attendance and punctuality.
options: Showing tolerance of and respect for the rights of others
Ensuring that personal beliefs are not expressed in ways which exploit pupils' vulnerability
Prioritising the academic progress of high-attaining pupils over the safety of others
Maintaining high standards in their own attendance and punctuality

bank.question: What is the primary purpose of 'scaffolding' in a lesson?
bank.explanation: Scaffolding is a temporary support mechanism that is gradually removed as the pupil gains independence and mastery
options: To provide temporary support that is gradually removed as learners gain mastery
To ensure that every student is doing a different task based on their ability
To provide pupils with the correct answers before they attempt a task
To separate high-attaining pupils from low-attaining pupils during lessons

bank.question: 'Assessment for Learning' (AfL) is synonymous with summative assessment, as both aim to provide a final grade for a unit of work
bank.explanation: Formative assessment is the 'assessment for learning' that happens during the process; summative assessment measures what has been learned at the end

bank.question: Which of the following best describes the technique of 'elaborative interrogation'?
bank.explanation: Elaborative interrogation involves students explaining why a fact or concept is true, which helps integrate new info with existing knowledge
options: Asking students to repeat a series of facts until they are memorised
Testing students under high-pressure exam conditions
Asking students to explain the 'how' and 'why' behind a specific concept
Providing students with pre-written summaries of a textbook chapter

bank.question: In Cognitive Load Theory, what does 'extraneous load' refer to?
bank.explanation: Extraneous load refers to unnecessary information that distracts from the actual learning goal
options: The inherent difficulty of the subject matter being taught
The mental effort required to store new information in long-term memory
Information or activities that distract from the primary learning goal
The physical exhaustion students feel at the end of a school day

bank.question: In the 'Instructional Framework', why is 'checking for understanding' vital during a lesson?
bank.explanation: Checking for understanding allows the teacher to identify and correct misconceptions before they become embedded in the student's long-term memory
options: To ensure the teacher can finish the lesson on time
To identify and address misconceptions before they become embedded
To provide a formal grade for the school's tracking system
To allow the most confident students to lead the classroom discussion

bank.question: Which two practices are key features of 'Adaptive Teaching' as described in the Early Career Framework?. (Select 2)
bank.explanation: Adaptive teaching involves high expectations for all, adjusting the support provided rather than reducing the difficulty of the task. The correct answers are Adjusting the level of support provided rather than the learning objective itself and Using flexible grouping based on current pupil understanding of a specific concept.
options: Adjusting the level of support provided rather than the learning objective itself
Creating entirely different lesson plans for four different ability groups in every lesson
Using flexible grouping based on current pupil understanding of a specific concept
Assigning 'easier' tasks to pupils with SEND to ensure they always finish first

bank.question: According to the Education Act 2002, what must a school's curriculum promote?
bank.explanation: A broad and balanced curriculum should promote the spiritual, moral, cultural, mental, and physical development of pupils
options: Spiritual, moral, cultural, mental and physical development
Academic attainment and high-stakes testing performance only
Preparation for university entry and vocational careers
British values, physical fitness, and digital literacy only

bank.question: Under UK safeguarding guidance, a teacher has a professional responsibility to share information with other agencies if they believe a child is at risk of harm
bank.explanation: The 'Working Together to Safeguard Children' statutory guidance states that any professional with concerns must share that information to protect the child

bank.question: In Cognitive Load Theory, what is the 'split-attention effect'?
bank.explanation: The split-attention effect occurs when students have to divide their attention between two or more related sources of information that are physically separated
options: When a student tries to listen to music while completing homework
When a teacher asks a question while students are writing an essay
When students are forced to work in groups of more than four people
When related information is physically separated on a page or screen

bank.question: What is the main pedagogical advantage of increasing 'Wait Time' after asking a question?
bank.explanation: The 'Wait Time' strategy gives students a few seconds to process a question, leading to more detailed and considered responses
options: It increases the length and quality of student responses
It discourages students from participating in class discussions
Shortening the time spent on a topic ensures the curriculum is covered
It is only useful for students with special educational needs

bank.question: What does 'overlearning' refer to in the context of skill acquisition?
bank.explanation: Overlearning-continuing to practice a skill after it has been mastered-is a key technique for achieving automaticity and fluency
options: Rereading a textbook several times without taking notes
Continuing to practice a skill after it has been perfectly performed once
Spending more than two hours on a single homework task
Learning information that is beyond the current curriculum level

bank.question: Which three strategies promote 'Metacognition' and self-regulated learning in the classroom?. (Select 3)
bank.explanation: Metacognition involves pupils understanding their own learning processes and being able to plan and evaluate their work. The correct answers are Explicitly teaching pupils how to plan a task before they begin, Encouraging pupils to monitor their progress against success criteria during a task and Reflecting on which strategies worked best after a task is completed.
options: Explicitly teaching pupils how to plan a task before they begin
Telling pupils exactly what to think so they do not make mistakes
Encouraging pupils to monitor their progress against success criteria during a task
Reflecting on which strategies worked best after a task is completed

bank.question: What is the main advantage of 'modelling' when introducing a complex task?
bank.explanation: Modelling involves the teacher 'thinking aloud' to make the invisible mental processes of an expert visible to the novice learner
options: Showing students a finished example of a high-quality essay
Ensuring the teacher is dressed in professional business attire
Demonstrating a process while 'thinking aloud' to show the steps involved
Using 3D models and physical props to explain abstract concepts

bank.question: According to research on effective feedback, telling a pupil they are 'naturally gifted' after a task is the best way to foster a growth mindset
bank.explanation: Feedback is most effective when it is specific and actionable; praising intelligence ('you are so smart') can actually discourage pupils from taking risks

bank.question: Which of these is a requirement of Part 1, Standard 1 of the UK Teachers' Standards?
bank.explanation: Teacher Standard 1 requires teachers to set high expectations which inspire, motivate and challenge pupils
options: Set goals that stretch and challenge pupils of all backgrounds and abilities
Focus primarily on the top 10% of high-attaining pupils
Ensure all pupils reach the same level of attainment by the end of the year
Avoid challenging pupils who have Special Educational Needs (SEND)

bank.question: Which of the following is a characteristic of a 'summative' assessment?
bank.explanation: Summative assessment evaluates student learning at the end of an instructional unit by comparing it against a benchmark
options: A teacher giving verbal feedback while a student is writing a draft
A 'thumbs up' check at the start of a lesson to gauge confidence
A formal end-of-year exam used to determine a final grade
An exit ticket used to plan the following day's lesson

bank.question: According to Rosenshine's Principles of Instruction, what is the optimal success rate for students during independent practice?
bank.explanation: Rosenshine's Principles emphasize that a high success rate (around 80%) helps build student confidence while ensuring tasks remain challenging
options: 100% Success rate to ensure no errors
Approximately 80% success rate
50% Success rate to maximize challenge
Success rates are not relevant to cognitive progress

bank.question: In the Ofsted Education Inspection Framework, which two factors are primary considerations within the 'Quality of Education' judgement?. (Select 2)
bank.explanation: The EIF focuses on the 'Quality of Education' which includes the curriculum design (intent) and how it is taught (implementation). options: The number of physical textbooks available in the school library
How the curriculum is designed to build knowledge over time (Intent)
The frequency of formal written reports sent to parents annually
How teachers deliver the curriculum and use assessment (Implementation)

bank.question: Which of the following is the best example of formative assessment?
bank.explanation: A low-stakes quiz is a common form of formative assessment used to monitor learning and provide ongoing feedback

A GCSE mock examination paper
An end-of-year formal report to parents
A key stage SATs examination

bank.question: In the context of the EEF Guidance Reports, what does the term 'metacognition' primarily refer to?
bank.explanation: Metacognition involves being aware of one's own thought processes and actively managing how one approaches learning tasks
options: The ability to memorize large amounts of data quickly
A teacher's ability to manage classroom behavior
A pupil's ability to monitor and direct their own learning
The process of grading a student's final portfolio

bank.question: Which statutory DfE document outlines the legal requirements for safeguarding in UK schools?
bank.explanation: The DfE 'Keeping Children Safe in Education' (KCSiE) guidance is the primary statutory document for school safeguarding

Keeping Children Safe in Education (KCSiE)
The Teachers' Standards (Part One)
The SEND Code of Practice

The Local Authority Liaison Officer

bank.question: Which three questioning techniques are most effective for checking pupil understanding during a lesson?. (Select 3)

Using 'Cold Call' to ensure all pupils are ready to respond, not just volunteers

bank.question: Which of the following best defines 'retrieval practice'?

options: Bringing information to mind from memory to strengthen storage
Reading a textbook chapter multiple times to memorize it
Summarising notes into a shorter format using a highlighter
Watching a video demonstration of a skill twice

bank.question: What does 'retrieval practice' involve to help strengthen long-term memory?
bank.explanation: Cognitive search occurs when a student tries to retrieve a memory, which actually strengthens the neural pathway for that information
options: Repeatedly reading a textbook passage to ensure it is memorised
Listening to a teacher explain a concept for the second time
Highlighting key vocabulary in a printed paragraph
Recalling information from memory without the help of notes

bank.question: Which part of the Teachers' Standards specifies that teachers must maintain appropriate boundaries with pupils?

bank.question: Regarding 'curriculum sequencing', which two principles help pupils build a coherent schema of knowledge?. (Select 2)

Ensuring that new content relates to and builds upon what has been taught previously
Sequencing concepts so that prerequisite knowledge is mastered before moving on
Covering as many topics as possible at a surface level to ensure curriculum breadth

bank.question: What is the main purpose of using 'concrete examples' in teaching?
bank.explanation: Concrete examples help students understand abstract concepts by providing a clear, relatable reference point

To ensure students only learn one specific application of a rule
To test if students can draw accurately
To help students understand abstract ideas through familiar contexts

bank.question: One of Rosenshine's Principles of Instruction suggests that daily review is essential for helping pupils connect new learning to prior knowledge

bank.question: What are the four stages of the 'graduated approach' described in the SEND Code of Practice?

options: Assess, Plan, Do, Review
Observe, Record, Grade, Report
Identify, Test, Assist, Graduate
Listen, Model, Practise, Feedback

bank.question: Under the UK Teachers' Standards, 'Standard 2' requires teachers to do what?

Set high expectations which inspire, motivate and challenge
Manage behaviour effectively to ensure a good and safe learning environment
Failing to plan lessons that are structured and sequenced

bank.question: What does the term 'circulation' refer to in classroom management?

options: Standing at the front of the class at all times
Sitting at the teacher's desk to mark books during independent work
Strategically moving around the classroom to supervise and support
Leaving the room to check on other classes

options: It should be sustained over a period of time rather than a 'one-off' event
It should focus solely on administrative tasks to save time
It should involve collaboration with peers and expert challenge

bank.question: Which of the following is a key feature of 'Cold Calling' as a questioning technique?

Phoning parents during the lesson to discuss behavior
Asking a question and allowing the whole class to shout out the answer
Asking a student by name to answer a question regardless of whether their hand is up

bank.question: The Teachers' Standards (Part Two) specify that a teacher's personal conduct only matters during school hours and has no relevance in their private life

bank.question: What is the legal duty of a school toward pupils with a disability under the Equality Act 2010?

Substantial changes to the building infrastructure regardless of cost
Exemption from the national curriculum for all disabled pupils

High-frequency academic words found across many subjects (e.g., 'interpret')
Slang or informal language used by students in the playground

bank.explanation: The 'Working Memory' is the system responsible for holding and processing limited information temporarily before it is encoded into long-term memory

Long-term memory
Working memory

Removing all teacher support immediately after introduction
Providing opportunities for guided practice before moving to independent work

bank.question: What is the pedagogical purpose of 'Dual Coding'?

Assigning two teachers to the same group of students
Teaching a lesson in two different languages simultaneously
Repeating the same information twice using different words

bank.question: Low-stakes testing, such as a quick quiz at the start of a lesson, is an effective form of retrieval practice that aids long-term memory

bank.question: Which of the UK Teachers' Standards states that a teacher must 'manage behaviour effectively to ensure a good and safe learning environment'?

options: Standard 1
Standard 3
Standard 5
Standard 7

bank.question: What is the purpose of 'Guided Practice' in a structured lesson sequence?

options: Students are given a worksheet to complete in total silence
The teacher and students work through a problem together on the board
The teacher stands at the front and talks for the entire lesson
Students are left to discover the rules of a subject on their own

bank.question: What does the 'spacing effect' (also known as distributed practice) refer to?
bank.explanation: Spacing involves spreading out study or practice over time rather than 'cramming' it into one block, which leads to better long-term retention
options: Focusing on one topic for an extended, continuous period
Distributing practice of a topic over a period of time
Providing physical distance between students during an exam
Adding blank spaces in worksheets for students to write in

bank.question: Which three strategies are most effective for establishing a positive classroom climate at the start of a school year?. (Select 3)

Maintain high expectations for all pupils' behaviour and effort
Use positive reinforcement and praise to reward desired behaviours
Ignore low-level disruption to avoid interrupting the lesson flow

bank.question: What is the purpose of a 'Think-Aloud' during the modelling phase of a lesson?
bank.explanation: A 'Think-Aloud' allows the teacher to make their thinking process visible, showing students how to approach a problem or task
options: Testing students on their prior knowledge before a unit starts
Asking students to whisper their answers to a partner
The teacher narrating their thought process while modelling a task
Encouraging students to shout out answers to build confidence

bank.question: If a teacher confiscates a mobile phone as a disciplinary penalty, they are legally entitled to keep the device permanently
bank.explanation: Keeping the phone might be a temporary measure for safety, but it remains the pupil's property; it must be returned as soon as is reasonable

bank.question: To whom should a teacher first report a safeguarding concern about a child, according to statutory guidance?
bank.explanation: The Designated Safeguarding Lead (DSL) is the person responsible for receiving reports and managing safeguarding concerns within a school
options: The Designated Safeguarding Lead (DSL)
The Chair of Governors
The Local Authority Liaison Officer (LADO)
The Head of Department

bank.question: What does the acronym 'EHCP' stand for in the context of Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND)?
bank.explanation: The EHCP is a legal document describing a child's needs and the support required to meet them
options: Education, Health and Care Plan
Extra Help for Children and Parents
Effective Holistic Care Programme
Essential Habilitation for Child Progress

bank.question: What is 'Interleaving' in the context of student practice?
bank.explanation: Interleaving involves mixing different topics or problem types within a single practice session, which helps students distinguish between concepts
options: Completing all practice for one topic before moving to the next
Using different fonts and colours to distinguish between handouts
Mixing different topics or problem types within a practice session
Providing students with a breakdown of their exam grades

bank.question: Which two approaches are recommended for supporting pupils who have English as an Additional Language (EAL)?. (Select 2)
bank.explanation: EAL learners benefit from visual clues and key vocabulary lists to bridge language gaps without lowering academic rigor. The correct answers are Provide visual scaffolds and graphic organisers to support meaning and Pre-teach key vocabulary and 'tier 2' words before the main lesson.
options: Provide visual scaffolds and graphic organisers to support meaning
Provide simplified texts that lower the cognitive challenge
Pre-teach key vocabulary and 'tier 2' words before the main lesson
Avoid using the pupil's home language during any task

bank.question: What is the main objective of the Pupil Premium funding in UK schools?
bank.explanation: The primary goal is to close the attainment gap between disadvantaged pupils and their peers by providing targeted support
options: To pay for generic school administrative costs and overheads
To close the attainment gap between disadvantaged pupils and their peers
To provide free school meals for all pupils in the school
To fund international school trips for high-achieving students

bank.question: Direct or explicit instruction is usually more effective than unguided 'discovery learning' when pupils are first introduced to a new, complex topic
bank.explanation: Explicit instruction is particularly beneficial when pupils are learning brand new, complex concepts where they have little prior knowledge

bank.question: Which of the following best describes 'Assessment for Learning' (AfL)?
bank.explanation: Formative assessment is the ongoing monitoring of student learning to provide feedback and inform future teaching
options: Assessment that occurs only at the end of a GCSE course
A formal ranking system to compare students against the national average
A method for deciding which students receive special education funding
Ongoing assessment used to adapt teaching to meet student needs

bank.question: What is a core component of 'Self-Regulation' in pupils?
bank.explanation: Self-regulation involves pupils being aware of their own learning processes and choosing strategies to overcome challenges
options: Students remaining silent throughout the entire school day
A teacher choosing every task for the student to complete
Only allowing students to work individually without any peer support
Students monitoring their own progress and adjusting their strategies

bank.question: Which statutory duty requires teachers to be alert to the signs of radicalisation and extremism?
bank.explanation: The PREVENT duty requires schools to have due regard to the need to prevent people from being drawn into terrorism
options: The PREVENT duty
The British Values mandate
The Counter-Terrorism Act 2015 Amendment
The Safeguarding Vulnerable Groups Act

bank.question: Which three features are characteristic of a 'Systematic Synthetic Phonics' (SSP) approach?. (Select 3)
bank.explanation: A phonics-led approach ensures children can decode before moving on to higher-level reading skills. The correct answers are Teaching pupils to blend sounds (phonemes) to read words, Ensuring books are closely matched to the phonics knowledge of the pupil and Directly teaching 'Grapheme-Phoneme Correspondences' (GPCs).
options: Encouraging children to guess words based on the pictures
Teaching pupils to blend sounds (phonemes) to read words
Ensuring books are closely matched to the phonics knowledge of the pupil
Directly teaching 'Grapheme-Phoneme Correspondences' (GPCs)

bank.question: What is a 'hinge question' in the context of a lesson?
bank.explanation: Hinge questions are diagnostic tools used at a specific point in a lesson to check if students have understood a concept before moving on
options: Open-ended questions designed to start a debate
Questions asked at the very beginning of a lesson to check attendance
Diagnostic questions used to decide whether to move on or reteach a concept
Questions used exclusively for summative end-of-year examinations

bank.question: Maintained schools in England are not required to have a 'Designated Teacher' for looked-after children (LAC)
bank.explanation: A designated teacher (DT) must be appointed to promote the educational achievement of looked-after and previously looked-after children

bank.question: In the context of educational theory, what does the term 'pedagogy' specifically refer to?
bank.explanation: The 'curriculum' represents what is taught, whereas 'pedagogy' describes the methods and practices used by the teacher to deliver that content
options: The specific order in which topics are taught
The assessment tools used to measure progress
The methods and practices used by teachers to deliver instruction
The statutory list of subjects required by law

bank.question: In the context of cognitive science and pedagogy, what does 'Dual Coding' involve?
bank.explanation: Dual coding is the process of combining verbal and visual information to help students process information through two different channels, reducing cognitive load and improving recall
options: Teaching the same lesson to two different ability groups simultaneously
Providing two different worksheets for every task to ensure variety
Combining words and visuals to help students process information more effectively
Ensuring a lesson is taught by two qualified teachers at the same time

bank.question: Under the UK government's statutory guidance, what is the primary definition of 'Early Help'?
bank.explanation: The 'Working Together to Safeguard Children' guidance defines 'Early Help' as providing support as soon as a problem emerges at any point in a child's life
options: Providing support as soon as a problem emerges at any point in a child's life
Support given only to children under the age of five
The final stage of intervention before legal action is taken
A specific programme for children with physical disabilities only

bank.question: Which two methods are proven by cognitive science to improve long-term memory retention?. (Select 2)
bank.explanation: Retrieval practice and spacing help strengthen long-term memory according to cognitive science research. The correct answers are Retrieval practice: bringing information to mind from memory and Spaced practice: revisiting content at increasing intervals over time.
options: Retrieval practice: bringing information to mind from memory
Blocked practice: focusing on one topic for a long period
Massed practice: 'cramming' all learning into a single session
Spaced practice: revisiting content at increasing intervals over time

bank.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the three types of cognitive load identified by John Sweller?
bank.explanation: Cognitive Load Theory identifies intrinsic load (task difficulty), extraneous load (delivery method), and germane load (processing needed to learn). Extension load is not a term used in this theory
options: Intrinsic load
Extraneous load
Germane load
Extension load

bank.question: The SEND Code of Practice states that high-quality teaching, differentiated for individual pupils, is the first step in responding to pupils who may have SEN
bank.explanation: The SEND Code of Practice outlines high-quality 'quality first' teaching as the fundamental first step in responding to pupils who have or may have SEN

bank.question: What is the main purpose of 'scaffolding' in a classroom setting?
bank.explanation: Scaffolding provides temporary support that is gradually removed as the pupil gains independence, consistent with Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development
options: Giving students the answers at the beginning of the task
Providing temporary support that is removed as a pupil gains mastery
Grouping students by ability for every lesson
Removing all difficult vocabulary from a text to make it easy to read

bank.question: What is the 'Halo Effect' in an educational assessment context?
bank.explanation: The 'Halo Effect' is a cognitive bias where a teacher's overall positive impression of a student in one area (e.g., behaviour) influences their evaluation of that student in another area (e.g., academic work)
options: The tendency for a teacher's overall impression of a student to influence their assessment of that student's work
A method of classroom management that uses positive reinforcement exclusively
The practice of seating high-attaining pupils next to low-attaining pupils to provide support
A specific lighting technique used in drama lessons to signify a character's innocence

bank.question: According to Part 1 of the Teachers' Standards, what is a key requirement for 'Setting high expectations' (Standard 1)?
bank.explanation: While teachers should build relationships, Standard 1 specifically highlights the need for a safe and stimulating environment that inspires pupils
options: To maintain high standards of ethics and behaviour within the profession
To design and produce high-quality homework for all year groups
To establish a safe and stimulating environment for pupils, rooted in mutual respect
To ensure that all pupils achieve an 'A' grade in national examinations

bank.question: Under the 'Keeping Children Safe in Education' (KCSIE) guidance, what are three core elements of the definition of 'Safeguarding'?. (Select 3)
bank.explanation: Safeguarding covers actual harm, the risk of harm, and the general well-being of the child. The correct answers are Protecting children from maltreatment, Preventing impairment of children's mental and physical health and Ensuring children grow up in circumstances consistent with safe and effective care.
options: Protecting children from maltreatment
Preventing impairment of children's mental and physical health
Ensuring children grow up in circumstances consistent with safe and effective care
Restricting children's access to all forms of social media

bank.question: Which of the following best describes the concept of 'Metacognition'?
bank.explanation: Metacognition is often simplified as 'thinking about thinking' and involves pupils monitoring and directing their own learning
options: The ability of pupils to monitor, direct, and review their own learning
A strategy used to manage disruptive behaviour in the playground
The process of memorising facts through physical movement
A theory regarding the development of motor skills in early years

bank.question: Metacognition refers specifically to the biological process of physical brain development in adolescents
bank.explanation: Metacognition is actually 'thinking about thinking'-the ability of pupils to monitor, direct, and evaluate their own learning processes

bank.question: What does the term 'overlearning' refer to in cognitive science?
bank.explanation: Overlearning involves continuing to practice a skill or piece of information after it has been initially mastered to strengthen long-term retention
options: Studying for too many hours without taking a break
Attempting tasks that are far beyond a pupil's current ability level
The process of learning too many different subjects in one day
Practising a skill beyond the point of initial mastery to improve automaticity

bank.question: In a UK school setting, which level of Disclosure and Barring Service (DBS) check is mandatory for staff in 'regulated activity' with children?
bank.explanation: According to the Department for Education (DfE), any person who is in 'regulated activity' with children (work that involves close contact or supervision) must undergo an Enhanced DBS check
options: A Standard DBS check
An Enhanced DBS check with Children's Barred List check
A Basic DBS check from the local police station
A character reference from a former employer only

bank.question: Which of the following best defines 'self-efficacy' in a learning context?
bank.explanation: Self-efficacy, a term championed by Albert Bandura, refers to a pupil's belief in their own ability to succeed in specific tasks
options: A pupil's general level of self-esteem
A pupil's belief in their ability to succeed in specific tasks or situations
The teacher's ability to manage a classroom effectively
The physical health and well-being of a student

bank.question: Which two practices ensure that Teaching Assistants (TAs) are used effectively in the classroom, according to the EEF?. (Select 2)
bank.explanation: Teaching assistants are most effective when supporting learning rather than just supervising or doing tasks for pupils. The correct answers are Using TAs to lead small-group interventions with clear learning goals and Training TAs to scaffold and encourage pupil independence.
options: Assigning the TA to work exclusively with the same SEND pupil every lesson
Using TAs to lead small-group interventions with clear learning goals
Ensuring TAs provide the 'answers' to struggling pupils to build confidence
Training TAs to scaffold and encourage pupil independence

bank.question: What is the 'split-attention effect' in the context of instructional design?
bank.explanation: The 'split-attention effect' occurs when pupils are forced to toggle between two separate sources of information (e.g., a diagram and its legend) to understand the content
options: When pupils must divide their attention between two related sources of information to understand them
When a teacher speaks while pupils are reading a different text
The ability of a teacher to watch two different groups of students at once
A technique used to help pupils focus on two subjects simultaneously

bank.question: The Governing Body of a maintained school is responsible for the day-to-day management of the school and the direct supervision of teaching staff
bank.explanation: While parents are key stakeholders, the headteacher or a designated staff member is responsible for the overall curriculum and day-to-day management

bank.question: What is 'Quality First Teaching' as defined in the context of SEND?
bank.explanation: The SEND Code of Practice states that most pupils with SEND should be taught in mainstream classrooms via 'Quality First Teaching' that is adapted for their needs
options: A separate curriculum for pupils with special educational needs
Instruction delivered only by Teaching Assistants in small break-out rooms
High-quality inclusive teaching that is differentiated and personalised for all pupils
A specific high-intensity intervention programme for literacy only

bank.question: What is 'metacognition' in a classroom environment?
bank.explanation: Metacognition is often defined as 'thinking about thinking' and involves students monitoring, directing, and evaluating their own learning processes
options: The ability to memorise large amounts of factual data quickly
A teacher's ability to manage multiple classroom disruptions at once
The physical movements pupils make to represent abstract concepts
The ability of students to monitor and direct their own learning and thinking processes

bank.question: What is the primary characteristic of 'Formative Assessment'?
bank.explanation: Formative assessment is an ongoing process used to provide feedback and adjust teaching, whereas summative assessment evaluates learning at the end of a unit
options: Used at the end of a term to provide a final grade for a report
An ongoing process used by teachers to adapt teaching and learning to improve student outcomes
A national test taken by all pupils at age 11
An assessment conducted by external moderators to check school standards

bank.question: Regarding 'Remote Education', which three principles are emphasized in DfE guidance for maintaining high-quality learning?. (Select 3)
bank.explanation: Remote learning should match the quality of in-person teaching, though the delivery method changes. The correct answers are Prioritise high-quality explanations over the medium of delivery, Provide clear loops for assessment and feedback on remote work and Ensure tasks are adapted so pupils can access them at home.
options: Prioritise high-quality explanations over the medium of delivery
Ensure pupils spend at least 6 hours a day on a 'live' video link
Provide clear loops for assessment and feedback on remote work
Ensure tasks are adapted so pupils can access them at home

bank.question: What is considered the most effective type of feedback for pupil progress?
bank.explanation: According to the Education Endowment Foundation (EEF), feedback should be specific, encouraging, and focused on how the pupil can move forward in their learning
options: A numerical mark on every piece of work
A list of every error a pupil made during the task
General praise such as 'Good job' to boost confidence
Specific information regarding what a pupil has done well and clear next steps for improvement

bank.question: The 'spacing effect' suggests that learning is more effective when study sessions are spread out over time rather than crammed into a single session
bank.explanation: The 'forgetting curve' suggests that without review, information is quickly lost; spaced practice helps consolidate knowledge into long-term memory

bank.question: Which of the following describes the strategy of 'dual coding' to improve retention?
bank.explanation: The 'dual coding' theory suggests that combining verbal and visual information helps students process information more effectively in their working memory
options: Using two different teachers to explain a concept
Writing the same word in two different languages
Combining verbal explanations with relevant visual imagery
Teaching the same lesson twice to the same group

bank.question: What is the primary goal of 'scaffolding' in the classroom?
bank.explanation: Scaffolding refers to temporary supports (like sentence starters or word banks) that are gradually removed as a student becomes more independent and proficient
options: Temporary support provided to help a student complete a task they cannot yet do independently
The physical structures used to maintain safety during school building repairs
A permanent intervention for students with high-level special educational needs
The process of building a curriculum from the Foundation Stage up to Key Stage 4

bank.question: According to Barak Rosenshine's Principles of Instruction, what is the primary purpose of a daily review?
bank.explanation: Rosenshine's Principles suggest that frequent reviews help strengthen the retrieval paths in long-term memory, making future recall easier
options: To strengthen the retrieval of previous learning
To provide extra time for late-arriving pupils
To ensure every child has completed their homework
To formally grade every student's daily progress

bank.question: Which two statements correctly describe the principle of 'Dual Coding' in classroom instruction?. (Select 2)
bank.explanation: Dual coding combines words and images to reduce cognitive load and improve understanding. The correct answers are Presenting information using both verbal and visual formats and Ensuring visual aids are simple and directly related to the text.
options: Presenting information using both verbal and visual formats
Presenting information in at least three different languages
Ensuring visual aids are simple and directly related to the text
Filling every slide with as many images as possible

bank.question: In the context of the Early Career Framework, what is the core aim of 'adaptive teaching'?
bank.explanation: Adaptive teaching involves adjusting the support provided to ensure all students can meet the same high-level learning objectives, rather than lowering expectations
options: Providing different, easier learning objectives for lower-attaining students
Giving students different tasks based on their 'learning styles'
Reducing the curriculum content for students with SEND
Adjusting instruction so all pupils can access the same ambitious curriculum

bank.question: If a pupil makes a disclosure of physical abuse, the teacher should promise the pupil that they will keep the information a secret to maintain trust
bank.explanation: If a teacher has a safeguarding concern, they must follow the school's safeguarding policy, which usually involves' reporting it to the Designated Safeguarding Lead (DSL) immediately

bank.question: Who in a school has the primary responsibility for coordinating safeguarding and child protection?
bank.explanation: The Designated Safeguarding Lead (DSL) is the person responsible for managing and overseeing all safeguarding and child protection matters within a school
options: The Headteacher
The Designated Safeguarding Lead (DSL)
The Chair of Governors
The Local Authority Designated Officer (LADO)

bank.question: Which of the following best describes 'adaptive teaching' as outlined in the Early Career Framework?
bank.explanation: Adaptive teaching involves adjusting the speed or approach of a lesson in response to student understanding, rather than reducing expectations for certain groups
options: Creating entirely different lesson plans for every student in the class
Adjusting teaching during a lesson to meet the needs of all pupils without lowering expectations
Using technology to deliver lessons remotely to absent students
Only teaching students who have a diagnosed Special Educational Need (SEN) differently

bank.question: What does Cognitive Load Theory suggest is a major bottleneck in the learning process?
bank.explanation: Working memory has a very limited capacity; presenting too much new information at once can lead to cognitive overload, hindering learning
options: Long-term memory has a finite capacity for storing facts
Visual and auditory information are processed in the same 'channel'
Working memory can only hold a small amount of information at one time
Forgetfulness is primarily caused by a lack of effort from the learner

bank.question: Which three facts about 'Working Memory' are essential for teachers to understand when planning lessons?. (Select 3)
bank.explanation: Working memory is limited; teachers should avoid overwhelming it with too much new information at once. The correct answers are Working memory has a very limited capacity for new information, Working memory can hold an unlimited amount of data for several hours and Information in working memory must be processed to enter long-term memory.
options: Working memory has a very limited capacity for new information
Working memory can hold an unlimited amount of data for several hours
Breaking complex tasks into smaller chunks supports working memory
Information in working memory must be processed to enter long-term memory

bank.question: What is a common risk when an 'expert' teacher is explaining a new concept to a 'novice' pupil?
bank.explanation: The 'Expert-Novice' gap describes how experts automate processes, often making it difficult for them to remember the small, incremental steps a beginner needs to learn
options: An expert may overlook small steps that a novice needs to learn explicitly
Novices are generally less motivated to learn than experts
Experts have smaller working memory capacities than novices
The gap only applies to physical skills, not academic subjects

bank.question: Under the School Teachers' Pay and Conditions Document (STPCD), all teachers are entitled to a minimum of 10% of their timetabled teaching time for PPA
bank.explanation: PPA time must be at least 10% of a teacher's timetabled teaching time and is intended for planning, preparation, and assessment duties

bank.question: Which of the following is an example of 'retrieval practice'?
bank.explanation: Retrieval practice involves the act of recalling information from memory, which strengthens neural pathways and improves long-term retention
options: Re-reading a textbook chapter several times
Answering a quiz or test from memory
Highlighting key terms in a revision guide
Watching a video summary of a lesson topic
